pages.text: Look at the earth from space and what you see is mostly blue. More than 70 percent of the earth's surface is covered by ocean. If you filled the world's oceans into a container, they would hold approximately 1.335 billion cubic kilometres of water. The earth is, in every meaningful sense, a water planet.

image.note: Illustration: earth from space showing the blue dominance of oceans

pages.text: There are five named oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern, and the Arctic. In reality, they are all connected, forming one continuous body of water that flows around and between the continents. The Pacific is the largest, covering more area than all the world's landmasses combined. The Arctic is the smallest and the shallowest.

Nigeria sits on the Atlantic Ocean, on the Gulf of Guinea, in the curve of West Africa's coastline. The Atlantic has shaped Nigerian history: the same waters that carried slave ships in the eighteenth century carry oil tankers and container ships today. The sea has always been both a barrier and a route for the peoples of the Nigerian coast.

The ocean is never still. Great rivers of water, called currents, move heat around the planet, driven by winds, the earth's rotation, and differences in temperature and saltiness. The Gulf of Guinea has its own current, flowing eastward along the West African coast, shaping the region's fisheries and weather. Currents connect everything: a message in a bottle dropped off Lagos could, in time, wash up on a beach on the far side of the world.

Tides are the ocean breathing. Twice a day along the Nigerian coast, the sea rises and falls as the Moon's gravity sweeps the ocean around the turning earth. Fishing communities in the Niger Delta plan their whole day around the tide: when to launch, when to set nets, when a creek will be deep enough to pass. A tide table is as essential to a delta fisherman as a road map is to a lorry driver.
The ocean is not a single environment. It has zones, defined by depth, light, temperature, and pressure, each with its own community of living things.

image.note: Diagram showing ocean zones: sunlit zone, twilight zone, midnight zone, abyssal zone, with characteristic species at each level

pages.text: The sunlit zone, the upper 200 metres of the ocean, receives enough light for photosynthesis. Phytoplankton, microscopic plant-like organisms, produce oxygen and form the base of the ocean's food web. Every marine animal, from the smallest shrimp to the largest whale, depends ultimately on phytoplankton. They produce approximately half of all the oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.

Below the sunlit zone, the ocean darkens. In the twilight zone, from 200 to 1,000 metres, there is just enough light for some animals to see, but not enough for plants to grow. Many of the animals here are bioluminescent, producing their own light to attract prey or find mates in the dark. The hatchetfish, the lanternfish, and the firefly squid all produce light this way.

Below 1,000 metres, there is no light at all. The midnight zone and the abyss below it are perpetually dark, cold, and under enormous pressure. Yet life survives here too: strange, slow-moving creatures adapted to conditions that would crush a human body instantly. The giant squid, which can reach 13 metres in length, lives in these depths and is rarely seen.

The ocean's reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on earth. Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which secrete hard calcium carbonate skeletons. Over thousands of years, these skeletons accumulate to form enormous reef structures. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia is the largest living structure ever built on earth.

In 1977, scientists exploring the deep Pacific found something that rewrote biology: hot springs on the ocean floor, called hydrothermal vents, surrounded by thriving communities of giant tube worms, crabs, and shrimp. No sunlight reaches there. The entire food web runs on chemical energy from inside the earth, harvested by special bacteria. Until that moment, science assumed all life depended on the sun. The ocean's answer was: not necessarily.

The largest animal that has ever lived is alive right now. The blue whale, at up to thirty metres and nearly two hundred tonnes, outweighs the largest dinosaurs, yet it feeds almost entirely on krill, shrimp-like creatures the size of your little finger, filtering them from the water by the tonne. Whales pass through the Gulf of Guinea on their migrations, and humpback whales calve in the warm waters off the West African coast.

Nigeria's coastline extends for approximately 853 kilometres along the Gulf of Guinea. The coastal zone includes beaches, estuaries, mangrove forests, and the vast Niger Delta, one of the largest river deltas in the world and one of the most biodiverse coastal ecosystems in Africa.

The Gulf of Guinea is one of the most productive fishing grounds in West Africa. Millions of people across the region depend on its fish for food and income. Nigerian fishing communities along the coast and in the Niger Delta have fished these waters for generations. However, overfishing, pollution from oil extraction, and the effects of climate change are putting this resource under serious pressure.

image.note: Illustration of Niger Delta coastline: mangroves, fishing boats, river channels

pages.text: Oil was discovered in the Niger Delta in 1956, and since then the region has produced the great majority of Nigeria's oil export revenue. But oil production has come at an environmental cost. Oil spills, gas flaring, and the infrastructure of the oil industry have damaged mangroves, poisoned waterways, and harmed the fishing communities that depend on the delta's health.
Cross-reference: The Gulf of Guinea connects to the Atlantic Ocean. For more on the Atlantic's role in Nigerian history, see HAARAYA L11 Tafiya NF: How Nigeria Was Colonised.

Mangroves are the ocean's nursery and Nigeria's underrated treasure. These salt-tolerant trees, standing on stilt roots along the Niger Delta, form one of the largest mangrove forests in the world. Young fish shelter among the roots before moving to open water, so the mangroves quietly feed the entire coastal fishery. They also break storm waves, trap sediment, and store remarkable amounts of carbon. Cutting a mangrove is cutting the sea's food supply at its root.

Nigeria lives by its ports. Apapa and Tin Can Island in Lagos, together with newer ports such as Lekki, handle the ships that carry Nigeria's oil out and the world's goods in. Beyond the docks, the Nigerian Navy patrols the Gulf of Guinea, where piracy against ships has been a serious problem. A country with 853 kilometres of coast is a maritime nation whether it thinks of itself that way or not.

The world's oceans are under pressure from several directions simultaneously. Climate change is warming ocean water, which bleaches coral reefs, disrupts marine food chains, and raises sea levels. Overfishing has depleted fish populations that once seemed inexhaustible. Plastic pollution has entered every ocean on earth, from the surface to the deepest trenches.

Plastic is particularly damaging. More than eight million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean every year. Plastics break down into tiny fragments called microplastics, which are eaten by fish and other marine animals, entering the food chain and ultimately reaching the fish on people's plates. Microplastics have been found in human blood, in breast milk, and in the placentas of unborn children.

pages.text: Sea level rise, driven by the melting of polar ice and the thermal expansion of warming water, threatens Nigeria's coastline. Lagos, one of the world's largest cities, sits at sea level on a series of low-lying islands and lagoons. Flooding events in Lagos are already increasing in frequency and severity. Without significant adaptation, parts of the city face inundation in the coming decades.

The ocean has given the world its weather, its oxygen, much of its food, and the routes that connected human civilisations across centuries. Understanding it, and taking responsibility for its health, is not optional. The ocean is not separate from human life. It is the system that makes human life on this planet possible.

The ocean's future is being negotiated now. Nations have agreed a High Seas Treaty to protect life in waters beyond any country's borders, and campaigns continue to protect a third of the ocean by 2030. Nigeria's part is close to home: defending the mangroves, cleaning up the delta, policing its waters, and managing its fisheries so there are fish for the next generation. The sea has fed people for as long as there have been people. Kept healthy, it always will.
